title: A Crime in My Hand
blurb: A suspended clerk climbs the hill to a garden of illegal knots, and the only teacher who will take her asks her to sign her name to a crime.

blocks.text: Nettlecombe Allotments, in the rain, and a coin lands on its edge on a potting bench and stays there.
Starlings line the fence wire at exact intervals. My bob will not settle. It swings crooked, circles, and starts again, over every stone on the terrace.
Every one of them is a knot. Every one is illegal. I am suspended for far less.
A woman with a trowel looks up at me as if I were late.
"You're the clerk," she says. "Took you long enough."

It has been eight days since the Lantry Steps. I gave the review a week, because that is what you do: you wait for the letter, you keep your head down, you do not go up a hill to find a stranger's gardener. The review has given me nothing back. So here I am.
"I'm Ila Brandt," I say, and hold out my hand. "Mr Pargeter sent me. He said to ask for Orla."
She looks at my hand. She doesn't take it. She goes back to her weeding.
"Wait there," she says.
So I wait. The rain runs off the brim of my hood. I have been waiting all week, really, and lying all week too, and this morning was the worst of it.
This morning I stopped at Dad's lock-up on my way to not going to work.

It's the last one in the row of lock-ups off Tallow Row, with the door rolled half up and a radio on low. Dad was truing a bicycle wheel with the rim clamped between his knees, turning the spoke key with his right hand. His left hand rested on his thigh, the way it always rests. He lost the use of it thirty years ago, on the docks, he says, when he was a Porter. A chain came off a crane. That is the whole of the story, and when I ask for more of it, he talks about bicycles.
"Morning, Inspector," he said.

He has called me that since I was nine and told him his toolbox was a disgrace. He thinks I file claims for an insurance office on Quay Street. I let him think it. I left him off my application to the Bureau, because the rule is plain: Bureau staff with Porter family are barred, conflict of interest, no exceptions. So I have one secret from the Bureau, which is him, and one from him, which is the Bureau. And now a third, which is that the Bureau has sent me home.
I put his flask on the bench. "Busy day," I said.
"Claims?"
"Claims."
He looked at the front of my coat, where my pass usually hangs. "No pass?"
"In my bag."
He nodded, slowly, and spun the wheel and watched it wobble. "Somebody left this one out all winter," he said. "Look at the chain. You can't get rust like that by accident. You have to work at it."
And that was all. He didn't ask again. I kissed the top of his head, walked out in my work coat with my packed lunch, and caught the tram the other way, up the hill to here.
"Clerk," says the woman with the trowel. "You've a message."
I jump. I have been standing in her rain so long I've nearly forgotten the message.
"Yes! He said to tell you the umbrellas stopped."
She stops weeding. She doesn't look at me. She looks at a long flat stone at the edge of the bed, grey with a white seam through it.
"Hear that, Pilchard?" she says to it. "The umbrellas stopped."
There is a long pause. A coin falls off the bench, lands on its edge in the mud, and stays there.
"I know they did," she says.
"Then you know about Mr Pargeter? That his heart stopped, and they brought him back? I was the one who..."

"I don't discuss my neighbours." She stands, slowly, with a hand on her knee. She is older than I thought, seventy at least, in a waxed jacket gone pale at the seams. "Orla Treadgold. You've been swinging my garden from the gate for ten minutes. What does it tell you?"
I want to get this right. I want to get it so right she can't help being impressed.

"Every stone is a tied knot, parked," I say. "Stones are the safe anchor, because a stone has no stake. Nobody uses it, nobody loves it, so its coincidences harm nobody. A knot parked on a stone is loud and nothing more. Coins on their edges. Birds in a line. Nothing bigger than that, within about a hundred metres."
"And?"
"And any knotter with a bob could swing it from the lane, like I did. And unless you hold a licence, it's unlicensed knotting under the Incidental Matters Act. Are you licensed?"
"Are you?"
I open my mouth. I close it. I am a suspended Registry Clerk, and a Registry Clerk's licence is nought and nought.
"No," I say.
"Well, then." She picks up the long stone with the white seam and holds it out over the path. "If I untied Pilchard, here, now. Where would that land, do you suppose?"

"The slack would equal the knot's weight," I say at once. "It dwells at the site for one minute per strand. Then it falls on whoever signed the docket as keeper, some time in the next twenty-four hours, against the grain of what they intend. Distance doesn't matter."
"And if nobody signed?"
"Then the untier is the keeper."
"And if a boy climbs my fence tonight and pinches Pilchard?"
"Then the knot goes with him," I say. "And the loudness. Coins on his windowsill, birds on his gutter. A moved stone keeps the knot it had when it was lifted. Moving it never frees it."
She sets Pilchard down exactly where he was and pats him.
"Book," she says. "Book. Book. Book."
"It's all correct!"
"It is." She picks her trowel back up. "You know what it says. Not what it's for. A hundred and forty stones in this garden, Clerk, and don't you count them. They don't like it."

From the lane at the bottom of the terraces comes the clang of a tram bell and the sound of someone running. A young man in a courier's waterproof comes up the path between the beds at a trot, with a parcel under his arm and his phone in his hand. He stops at the potting bench, holds up the phone so Orla can see the time, and grins.
"Eleven-oh-four," he says. "You're welcome."
"Put it in the shed," says Orla.
He puts it in the shed. Then he sees me, and he grins at me too, because he's the sort of person who grins at whoever's there.
"Hello," I say. "I'm Ila. I'm new. Well, I'm not anything yet. I'm visiting."

"Ferdie," he says. "Ferdie Lusk. Brindlemouth Same-Day, Eastern Round. I came up on the 14 to Gullet Lane, cut through behind the chapel, up the terrace steps, which you shouldn't do in this weather because the third one rocks, and here at eleven-oh-four, which is when I said. Never been late in my life."
"Never?"

"Not once. Not a minute. Ask anybody." He's already checking his phone again. "Eleven-oh-six. I've got the docks at half past, then I'm off to pay my monthly. Cash only, can you believe it? In this day and age."
"That's very good timing," I say. "You must be the luckiest courier in Brindlemouth."
He goes quiet. Just like that, like a radio switched off. He looks at his phone, and not at me.
"Better go," he says. "Nice to meet you, Ila."
He trots off down the path. I watch him go, because I like him, and because I'm a little sorry about whatever I said.

At the bottom of the terraces a tram is pulling in at the stop on the lane. Ferdie reaches it just as the doors open, and hops on. The doors close behind him. A man in a grey suit comes running round the corner with his briefcase held up over his head, and reaches the stop just as the tram pulls away. One second. Maybe less. He stands in the rain with his briefcase still over his head and watches it go.
I notice it. I don't know what I notice, exactly. I keep it to myself.
When I turn round, Orla is watching the lane too. She doesn't say anything. She goes back to her bed.
Now. I have been rehearsing this part on the tram all the way up the hill.
"Mrs Treadgold," I say.
"Orla."
"Orla. I'd like you to teach me to trace."
That gets her attention. She sits back on her heels.

"I know the rule," I say, quickly, before she can ask. "You follow a strand backward one cause at a time, about a minute a link, slower when it branches. A strong knotter can trace about a day back in an hour. Past one year back is the Back Stair, and Standing Order One forbids it. I don't need anything like a year. I need a day."
"For what?"

"For whoever brought Mr Pargeter back." I can feel myself going too fast and I don't care. "Three things happened on those steps that nobody asked for. A nurse out of the tram queue. A defibrillator in the shelter. An ambulance already at the lights. Somebody arranged that. If I go back to the steps and pick up the ambulance's strand, or the nurse's, I can follow it back to the morning and find out who. A day. That's all. Well inside the order."
Orla looks at me for a long time. The rain ticks on the leaves. A starling drops onto the fence and lines itself up with the others.
"And where did the thing that saved him start," she says, "do you suppose?"
I go to answer, and nothing comes.

I think about the steps. The nurse cutting his shirt open. The scar, old and wide across his chest, and what she said over it: this heart should have quit years ago, something's been keeping it going. Something was holding his heart, for years. I untied the knot around it, and it let go, and in the same few minutes three things arrived that nobody could have arranged that morning, all at once, all exactly right, as if they had been waiting.
Waiting for the thing in his chest to let go.
Nobody fixes all that on the morning. You'd have to know a heart was going to stop, and when, and where. And the only way to know that is to have known about the heart all along.
"I'm wrong," I say, out loud. "It didn't start on the steps. It didn't start that day at all."
Orla says nothing. She pulls a weed and shakes the soil off its roots.
"Then I don't know how far back," I say. "Further than a day. I don't know how much further."
"No," says Orla. "You don't." She drops the weed in her bucket. "So here's your first lesson, Clerk, and you'll have it for free. Never trace past a year. Whatever you're after. Whoever."
"Standing Order One," I say.

"I don't care about orders. I care about the way back up." For the first time her voice isn't blunt. It's quiet. "Down there the strands thin out into millions. Only the heaviest will hold you. You lose count. You lose your head. You lose which way is up. The Back Stair has no banister."

I want to ask her how she knows. I can see from her face that it's the question she's hoping I won't ask, so of course I nearly do. Then the coin on the bench tips over at last, and she stands up, and the moment's gone.
"You'll teach me, then?"
"I didn't say that."
"But you gave me a lesson."

"I gave you a warning. A lesson costs." She walks along the edge of the bed, past Pilchard, past a fat round stone she calls Duchess and a small speckled one she calls Bun, until she stops at a row of cobbles along the path. She bends and picks one up, brown and smooth and the size of a large potato, and weighs it in her hand.
"Reach?" she says.
"Two. From the frames in the Registry basement. Four years of drills."

"Then here's a two." She puts the cobble in my palm. It's cold and wet, and it sits there as if it has always been mine. "I'll teach you. One condition. You untie this, here in my garden, in front of me. With a fid I lend you. You sign the docket yourself, as keeper, in your own hand."
"And the slack?"
"Is yours. Whatever it sends you, Clerk, it sends to you."

I look down at the cobble. Two strands. Inside my reach. Lawful under an emergency warrant, and I have no warrant. I have no licence. I have a suspension letter coming and a father I lied to over breakfast.
"That's unlicensed knotting," I say. "Under the Act. That's a crime."
"Yes," says Orla. She waits. She is very good at waiting. "Well?"
The Bureau sent me home for a drawer full of paper, and the first knotter who will teach me has just put a real crime in my hand and asked me to sign my name to it.
